extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for designing, manufacturing, and selecting books (typography, format, materials, binding, and production workflow), with guidance for publishers, printers, librarians, and informed consumers. Emphasizes durability, proportion, aesthetic utility, and the shared responsibilities of all parties in the production chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and size appropriate to purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose book size and format that suit the book's function and audience (e.g., Aldus octavo/sixteenmo and Elzevir pocket editions for portability and low price).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic examples (Aldus, Elzevirs, Blue and Gold, Little Classics, Tauchnitz) show that small, well-proportioned volumes served scholars and travelers and increased access. Consider portability, shelf-space economy, commercial price, and the intended reader when selecting format; recombining proven elements can recreate their appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of beauty and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-made book should unite aesthetic beauty and practical usefulness so that neither clearly dominates the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aldus's pages are praised as 'a union of beauty and utility' — aim for high standards in both form and function so a reader cannot decide which is pre-eminent. Design decisions should serve readability and handling as well as visual charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page proportions and classical grammar of page design
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain harmonious page proportions, including the relation of page length to width and margins shaped by classical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting tradition: 'that the length of a printed page should have relation to its width, and that the top should not exceed half the bottom margin, and that the front should be double the back margin.' Use established proportional relationships rather than arbitrary equal margins; compare samples and settle proportions before composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate type choice and size relative to page
rubrics_metrics.description: Select type and point size that suit the printed page — avoid type too large for the page and preserve readability and visual balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'book of to-day' is criticized for 'type too large for the page' producing poor esthetic effect. Study historic good examples (Aldus, Pickering) and test type/page combinations before committing to presswork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margins, catchwords, and typographic conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply considered typographic details (capitals, initials, italic use, catchwords) in ways that serve design coherence and reader convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Aldus used undersized roman capitals, printed a letter in the blank square to indicate the illuminator's initial, and placed the catchword only on the last page of the signature. Modern practice (e.g., subordinate use of italic) should be deliberate and justified by aesthetics and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper quality and durability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use good, durable paper suitable for the intended life of the book and the needs of libraries and readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor paper forces early rebinding and increased library costs; the papermaker is blamed for many spoiled books but ultimate remedy lies with consumers who must insist on durable paper. Libraries may accept slightly higher first cost to avoid rebinding soon after acquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ink quality and permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ inks that remain bright and clean over time; avoid sallow or chemically unstable inks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic inks have remained beautiful for centuries; modern 'sallow inks' offend sight and smell and degrade appearance. Ink choice is a fundamental component of craft—insist on stable formulations from ink-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding strength and longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide binding strong enough for repeated use; weak or cheap binding that fails after few readings is unacceptable for books meant to be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak bindings increase library rebinding expense; some publishers now cater to library demand by offering sturdier binding even at slightly higher first cost. Binding is one of the final critical stages where books are 'spoiled' if mishandled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good presswork and overall craftsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure high standards of presswork (even impression, registration, clean printing) and overall workmanship throughout production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many modern books may have 'clear type, black ink, and good presswork' as their redeeming merits, but presswork must be combined with proportion and materials. Examples: Pickering and Chiswick Press practices emphasized careful preparation and collaboration before composition to ensure craftsmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding superficial commercial puffery in form
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not design books to appear larger or more substantial than they are; avoid using size or showy covers to create illusion of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'book of to-day' is criticized for appealing to 'the primitive instinct for bigness'—design should not be based on what a book can be made to seem but on what it truly is. Publishers should resist deceptive formatting that prioritizes appearance over intrinsic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost is not a valid excuse for poor construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful and durable book does not necessarily cost materially more than a clumsy and unsightly one; cost alone should not justify poor manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Henry Stevens: 'The manufacture of a beautiful and durable book costs little if anything more than that of a clumsy and unsightly one.' Publishers and consumers should not accept the claim that good workmanship is unaffordable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinated responsibility across the production chain ('ten tribes')
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality depends on collaboration among author, publisher, printer, reader, compositor, pressman/machinist, papermaker, ink maker, bookbinder, and consumer — failures can originate in any party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stevens lists ten parties who 'spoil' books and diagnoses typical faults (e.g., author meddling, publisher ignorance, compositor overloaded, ink-maker producing poor inks). Remedy requires education, better instruction (school of typography), and consumers insisting on quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skilled compositor and thoughtful make-up
rubrics_metrics.description: The compositor (and those who set pages) must be trained and given time to create the book's actual form; compositors often determine the book's appearance and should be properly instructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositors should not be forced to assume multiple roles; they ought to attend a 'school of typography' and be better instructed in their trade and the essentials of book form before setting type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design process: collaborative pre-press planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers and printers should rigorously plan and agree on ideal form and proportions before composition begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pickering and Whittingham's practice of sitting 'upon every new book' and comparing sample leaves over days exemplifies how taking time to settle shape and dress yields excellence; emulate such pre-press collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate and cultivate reader/consumer taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Create demand for better books by educating book buyers: agitate (proclaim the lore), illustrate (show good and bad examples), and vindicate (support publishers who produce good books).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'book of to-morrow' will rely on an appreciative public; individual enlightened booklovers carrying out this plan could spark a revolution toward better and cheaper good books. Libraries and informed consumers play a crucial role by preferring quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for library use and space economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider library needs (durability, shelf-space economy, and long-term cost) when designing books; format and quality choices should reflect institutional use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public libraries face duplicated costs from rebinding and housing oversized books; some publishers now cater to library demand by producing sturdier bindings and more space-efficient formats. Standardization of sizes should be approached cautiously—only adopt sizes rooted in long public favor, not mechanical convenience alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genuinely artful editions from mere carriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether an edition is a genuine art product (careful design, proportions, craftsmanship) rather than merely a convenient carrier of text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author compares Little Classics (genuine art products) to Tauchnitz editions (mere carriers). Criteria include proportion, printed-page design, colored edges, and overall esthetic intent rather than mere low cost or portability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endurance and timelessness as design goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for designs that will endure aesthetically and materially over generations, as exemplified by Alduses and Elzevirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-designed volumes maintain charm and usefulness across centuries; consider long-term durability of materials and timelessness of proportions and typesetting when planning editions.
